title: A night at the museum: Dare to come face to face with a ghost at this year's Entler Hotel paranormal tour?
excerpt: Thousands of people have been in and out of the historic Entler Hotel Complex on East German Street in Shepherdstown, but some have never left. Possible encounters with their spirits
content:
Thousands of people have been in and out of the historic Entler Hotel Complex on East German Street in Shepherdstown, but some have never left. Possible encounters with their spirits are part of the Shepherdstown Museum’s ghost tour and, for those willing to take the chance and actually meet a ghost, the paranormal tour of the historic Entler Hotel and museum. The ghost tour is Oct. 24 and Oct. 31, while the paranormal tour is Oct. 24 and Oct. 30. 

The three-story museum was originally built as a private residence in 1786 and became part of the Entler Hotel in 1815. The Entler Hotel Complex includes several buildings and offices.

John Kavaliunas, who has been a docent of the museum for 14 years, said just about every room in the museum is reputed to have a ghost. He said he has never seen one, but when a film crew visited the museum, he did hear a spirit in one of their recordings.

That ghost was William Payton Smith, a lawyer from Winchester, Va., who in 1809 had a duel with another lawyer, Joseph Holmes. Duels were not allowed in Virginia at that time (West Virginia was still part of Virginia), so the duel took place across the river from Shepherdstown in Maryland. Smith was shot, then taken to the Entler Hotel, where he died of his wounds. The recording by the film crew has a man saying, “I didn’t shoot.” 

Kavaliunas said he hears stories about ghosts from different visitors to the museum as well as psychics who have sensed spirits there. One of the most haunted rooms is the Traveler’s Room on the second floor. It may have been available to rent years ago. “It’s the only room with beds,” he reported. “People have walked into that room then walked right back out. I’ve been told there is tremendous sadness in the room. Visitors actually cry.”

He reported an older woman allegedly died in the room, a woman lost her baby there and psychics have said they sensed a man who wanted to commit suicide who was a traveling salesman in the 1840s.

Visitors can participate in a free ghost tour to explore the museum’s rooms every half hour from 1 p.m. to 3:30 p.m. on Oct. 24 and Oct. 31. For a $20 fee on Oct. 24 and Oct. 30 from 7 p.m. to 9 p.m., people can attempt “to track down a ghost” in the paranormal tour with paranormal investigators. This is the third year of the tour, which is a fundraiser for the museum. The tour includes psychic medium Angel Wells and dowser Les Johnson, who uses divining rods to indicate the presence of ghosts.

Paranormal investigators Patricia Marin and Meredith Moore will also be part of this tour. 

Moore has been doing ghost tours in Shepherdstown and Sharpsburg, Md., for 18 years. She reported she has had personal experiences with several of the museum’s spirits. She used to have an office on the second floor. “I heard footsteps that sounded like cowboy boots. One night I felt hands on my shoulders that pushed me out of the building as I was leaving,” Moore said.

She said the footsteps may be those of what’s referred to as “an angry man on the second floor,” but no one knows for sure. That spirit might be associated with the 1892 murder of Shepherdstown resident Susie Ferrell, who was murdered in town by Harry M.Smootz. Smootz shot her, then fled to the Entler Hotel where he told his brother what he had done. He was found guilty of murder and scheduled to be hanged but died in his cell.

If you’re not seeking ghosts, the museum, operated by Historic Shepherdstown, a nonprofit membership organization, has a plethora of historical artifacts and information about Jefferson County. But all in all, it is the perfect time of year to catch a real ghost in the act.
